description: Why a carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) is a prerequisite for effective climate policy: diverging national interests, carbon leakage evidence, and the climate club mechanism. Draft to be validated against json_structure.md.

sources.name: Nordhaus 2015
sources.description: Nordhaus, W. (2015): Climate Clubs: Overcoming Free-Riding in International Climate Policy. American Economic Review 105(4), 1339-1370. Finding: without sanctions on non-participants no stable coalition beyond minimal abatement; small trade penalties enable large stable coalitions with high abatement.

sources.name: Branger Quirion 2014b
sources.description: Branger, F. & Quirion, P. (2014): Would Border Carbon Adjustments Prevent Carbon Leakage and Heavy Industry Competitiveness Losses? Ecological Economics 99, 29-39. Meta-analysis of 25 studies, 310 estimates.

sources.name: Branger Quirion 2014a
sources.description: Branger, F. & Quirion, P. (2014): Climate Policy and the Carbon Haven Effect. WIREs Climate Change 5(1), 53-71.

sources.name: SEI et al. 2023
sources.description: SEI, Climate Analytics, E3G, IISD, UNEP (2023): The Production Gap Report 2023. Governments plan ~110% more fossil fuel production in 2030 than consistent with 1.5 C; none of 20 profiled producer countries committed to 1.5 C-aligned production cuts.

sources.name: World Bank 2025
sources.description: World Bank (2025): State and Trends of Carbon Pricing 2025. ~28% of global GHG emissions covered by a direct carbon price; average implemented price ~USD 19 per ton.
